   ,
   - A. Mele (2013), *A Structural Model of Segregation in Social Networks*,
   available at http://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2294957.

I?m trying to replicating Butts? analysis of the Krackhardt (1987) dataset
[library(NetData)] with R-Statnet.



Despite my best efforts, so far I couldn?t find a way to estimate an ERGM
according to Butts? approach, and I was wondering if anyone has any ideas
on how to programming Butts (2009) ERGM parameterization or if can point me
to existing clarifying references that can help me in writing the correct
script on Statnet.



Thank you in advance,

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

many thanks for your help on my previous questions,

I have one more question concerning the definition of the "decay" in the
gwdegree term.

I wish to run a model including gwdegree, gwdsp and gwesp. I have no
problem for gwdsp and gwesp terms, and the value of alpha does not have a
strong influence on the results as it was underlined previously in this
forum.

However, the decay parameter for the gwdegree has a strong influence on the
results.

I tried the procedure recommended by Goodreau et al. 2008 and detailed in
the book of Harris, chap.3, by increasing progressively the decay and alpha
parameters as follow:

M.1 <- ergm(net~edges+gwdegree (0,fixed=T) + gwdsp
(0,fixed=T)+gwesp(0,fixed=T))
M.2 <- ergm(net~edges+gwdegree (0.1,fixed=T) + gwdsp
(0.1,fixed=T)+gwesp(0.1,fixed=T))
M.3 <- ergm(net~edges+gwdegree (0.2,fixed=T) + gwdsp
(0.2,fixed=T)+gwesp(0.2,fixed=T))
etc.. up to decay and alpha =1.1

My first question is whether I am right to use this procedure, considering
the three terms together ?

Models start to show signs of degeneracy for very low values of alpha and
decay (0.2), so in fact, the only models which are not degenerated are for
alpha/decay = 0.1 or 0 ...

I tried CEF models, but they showed signs of degeneracy.

Can anybody help me on this topic and share experience concerning the model
specification with these terms ?

Many thanks


Vanesse Labeyrie
post-doctoral fellow at UMR AGAP, CIRAD, France

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vanessa,

I have not spent much time working with gwdegree myself.  But I can 
share an experience with gwesp that may be of use.  The more I have 
worked with users troubleshooting their data, the more I have found that 
a higher alpha is often useful for gwesp when the data are more dense.  
In my own domain I mostly work with sparse data, and that is also the 
case in the Goodreau et al. 2008 paper.  Since then I have come to 
realize how things can be more complicated than that, and at least for 
gwesp, for dense data the lowest alphas can indeed cause problems.

You might try fixing the gwesp and gwdsp alphas, given your previous 
findings, but let the gwdegree one vary (with fixed=F) and see if the 
algorithm is able to find the MLE.  Given that there seems to be more 
impact for this value in your data than the others, there may well be 
plenty of information there for it to do the joint estimation easily.

I hope that helps a little,
Steve

Ok, many thanks to Steve and Martina for their help.

 I share my experience as it might interest other users,

The model I tried to fit was not able to converge when the decay parameter
of gwdegree was not fixed (CEF model),
so I adopted the method proposed by Hunter et al. 2008 and increased
progressively alpha (fixed =T), but for alpha > 0.1 for the three geometric

for gwdsp shall not exceed 0.1.

for the other geometric terms and the model with the best GOF in my case
was the one with alpha =0.1 for gwdegree and gwdsp and alpha=0.5 for gwesp.

alpha in terms of what patterns in the observed network are captured by 
allowing alpha to vary.

complete picture (see the documentation).

Martina

messages.body_plain:
Hi Statnet Users,

Admittedly, this question is a rehash of one asked by Brian Rubineau in 2007.  But when asked, David Hunter answered that it was unresolved (see https://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2007/000119.html).  This question has come up in my own research, and I was wondering if it had been resolved at this point in time.

Somewhat similar questions were asked in https://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2013/001493.html and https://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2010/000804.html.  The former received no answer and the latter requires a strong assumption (edge independence) and a quantitative (rather than categorical) variable.

I apologize for the lengthy documentation, though I wanted to demonstrate that I attempted to resolve this myself before turning to the statnet group.

I have data with one set of nodes and several sets of edges (5 to be exact - different areas of collaboration amongst entrepreneurs in developing countries).  I would like to compare the forces governing link formation in each network.  I have combined all my adjacency matrices into one big adjacency matrix (node names were adjusted to be unique; names are the original name + the network name).  This matrix is defined such that edges only exist between nodes from the same original network.

Ideally, this would mean constructing an ERGM with the same right-hand side (explanatory variables) for each network (different dependent variables, corresponding to each network), with the goal of comparing parameter estimates.  Comparing these parameter estimates would allow me to answer questions of the following form: Is transitivity stronger in one collaboration area versus another?

I'd like to adapt classical regression techniques by introducing dummy variables and interaction terms to statistically discern the differences in effects amongst the networks.  I've tried constructing a dummy variable off of my attribute list manually, and then including it in my ERGM, though I get an error and my code is not accepted by R.  I am also unable to multiply variables (as one must to construct an interaction term) in the ERGM function.

Thoughts?  Thank you for your time and consideration.

Cheers,
Louis

Hi, Louis.  What you are describing would be a pooled ERGM.  It can 
certainly be done, and papers on multiple-network ERGMs are starting to 
appear.  Software development has lagged somewhat, both because (1) 
there are so many things that need to be done on single-network ERGMs 
(and limited time to do it), and (2) there have been fewer available 
data sets to support model development than would be ideal.  This is 
something that some of us are actively working on, however, so the 
situation should be starting to change.

I have a prototype implementation of an ergm extension package that 
supports pooled ergms (and another for multiplex ergms, which is a 
special case that has somewhat different requirements). Right now, they 
are held together with twine and might set your hair on fire.  However, 
if you are potentially interested in being a beta tester for them when 
they are in a fit state for such, then send me a note off-list.

Hope that helps,

Hi Louis,

Just a few additional comments.

Since your networks are all the same size and composition, the question of 
comparability could be addressed in a more traditional fashion.  You could 
fit the same model to each network, and compare the transitivity 
coefficients by testing whether the differences between them are 
statistically significant, based on a t-test for differences, using the 
estimated SEs of each coefficient, and adjusting for multiple comparisons 
(presumably 5 choose 2 = 10 comparisons).

This doesn't incorporate the repeated measure design of your data (i.e., 
the consistent labeling of the nodes), but it would provide a network wide 
assessment of differences in transitivity.

As Carter noted, we have a number of projects in the pipeline that will 
extend ergm for multiple/multi-level networks.

best,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Sample Space is not dyad-independent
messages.body_plain:
Hi Thomas,

Thanks for asking. This is actually an example of a "good"warning that 
we put in there to be informative; it doesn't need to be fixed.  Some 
models are dyadic-independent, and others dyadic dependent, and this 
distinction leads to a number of important implications (e.g. whether 
MCMC is needed to fit the model).  This is a case where the model would 
be dyadic independent based on the terms in the formula, but because of 
the constraint it gets kicked into the category of dyadic dependent.  So 
we are pointing that out to people in case they have the wrong 
expectation based on the terms alone. There are also aspects of the 
statistical theory behind the models that works differently for models 
with dyadic dependent constraints. But again, you don't necessarily have 
to do anything about the warning.

I've seen other confusion around this as well, so I think we should 
probably change the warning to make it more clear, or perhaps remove it 
altogether.  I'll add it to our development team's decision list.

Thanks,
Steve

Hi Vanesse and all,

I recently did something similar to what you're proposing using BIC. It
seems to have worked for me, so I thought I'd throw it out here in case
it's useful to you or anyone thinks it was a bad idea (which I would
definitely like to hear about!).

I was only using two of those three parameters, but I fit ERGMs to my
networks using a full factorial crossing of potential decay parameter
values (along with other terms of interest). I took the combination of
decay parameter values that minimized BIC to be the best model. This was
computationally demanding even with just two GW-parameters, but if your
networks are smaller (mine were near 1000 nodes each times three networks),
it might not take too long.

Hope that helps,

Michael
